views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should hold firm on core interests while keeping the negotiating channel open, using the upcoming G20 as a potential off-ramp. Retaliate proportionally where necessary (the June 1 tariff hike on $60B US goods is already locked in), but avoid dramatic new escalations like a full rare-earth embargo before exhausting diplomacy. Signal willingness to talk while quietly preparing asymmetric countermeasures (rare earths, unreliable entity list) as leverage.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is substantial but not yet existential, warranting a +0.5 reading. Three factors drive this: (1) The tariff escalation is accelerating — the May 10 hike to 25% on $200B of goods and Trump's order to prepare tariffs on the remaining ~$300B would, if executed, cover virtually all Chinese exports to the US and could shave 1-1.5% off GDP (Barclays estimate, per Forbes 5/17). (2) The Huawei entity-list action (May 16) is a direct strike at China's tech champion — Google, Qualcomm, Microsoft, and ARM have suspended ties, threatening Huawei's $11B annual US component spend and its 5G/smartphone businesses. This goes beyond tariffs into industrial policy warfare. (3) China's May manufacturing PMI contracted (49.4 vs. 50.1 expected), with export orders declining for 12 straight months, suggesting the real economy is already feeling the bite.

However, several factors prevent a higher threat reading. China's Q1 GDP held at 6.4% (above consensus), the RMB's 8.2% depreciation since 2018 partially offsets tariff costs, and Beijing retains fiscal/monetary stimulus room. Xi's May 20 visit to a rare-earth facility in Jiangxi signaled that China holds asymmetric countermeasures — it controls ~80% of global rare earth supply, critical to US defense and tech sectors. The 'unreliable entity list' announced May 31 also gives Beijing a tool to pressure US firms dependent on the Chinese market.

The action_score of -0.15 reflects a posture of firm negotiation rather than fresh escalation. China has already retaliated (June 1 tariffs on $60B US goods), matching the US move. Further escalation — say, a full rare-earth cutoff — would risk triggering the $300B tariff tranche and accelerating supply-chain decoupling, which would hurt China more in the medium term. But full concession is also inappropriate: the structural issues (IP transfer, industrial subsidies, Made in China 2025) go to the core of China's development model and CCP legitimacy. The G20 meeting between Trump and Xi (expected late June) offers a natural venue for de-escalation, as the Buenos Aires precedent showed. China should engage there with concrete purchase commitments while holding the line on structural reforms.
key_factors: Tariff escalation to 25% on $200B (May 10) with $300B more threatened
Huawei entity-list (May 16) — existential threat to China's tech champion, $11B in US component dependency
May manufacturing PMI contraction (49.4) and 12-month decline in export orders
Rare earth leverage — Xi's Jiangxi visit signals potential countermeasure
Unreliable entity list (May 31) — new retaliation tool announced
RMB depreciation of 8.2% partially offsets tariff impact
Q1 GDP 6.4% beat expectations; stimulus space remains
G20 Trump-Xi meeting offers diplomatic off-ramp (Buenos Aires precedent)

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump tweets that negotiations are going 'too slowly' and that China is attempting to 'renegotiate.' Orders List 3 raised from 10% to 25% on May 10 and directs preparation of tariffs on remaining Chinese imports (~$300B).
US Commerce Department adds Huawei and affiliates to the Entity List. US firms generally barred from selling to Huawei without a license.

Google suspends Huawei's access to Android updates / GMS; major US chip suppliers pause sales. Same day: Xi Jinping visits a rare-earth facility in Jiangxi (widely read as a signal on rare-earth leverage).
China announces it will establish an 'unreliable entity list' targeting foreign firms that cut supplies to Chinese companies for non-commercial reasons.

China's factory activity in May slumped into a deeper contraction than markets had expected. Export orders extended their decline for the twelfth straight month with the sub-index pulling back significantly to 46.5 from April's 49.2.

Barclays Capital expects a one percentage point drop in China's GDP if Trump makes good on his promise to tax everything China sells to the U.S. at a rate of 25%. AXA: full-blown trade war will trim 1.5% off China's GDP.
Plans by Washington to hike tariffs on $200 billion of Chinese goods could cut China's growth by 0.3 percentage points, a Chinese central bank advisor said. 'This is within a controllable range.'
From March 2018 to May 2019, the RMB depreciated by 8.2%.

A major Chinese planning body has made a thinly-veiled threat to cut off the supply of rare earth minerals, used in a large variety of high-tech products, in response to the US move to ban the sale of vital high-tech products to Huawei.
